title: Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick
abstract: Marketers have never had more data to act on. Take an apparel brand that advertises on Meta technologies: campaign results live in Meta Ads Manager, briefs and creative assets in shared storage, and inventory, customer lifetime value, and in-store purchases in a data lake. Analysts export reports, merge spreadsheets, and rebuild the same deck each week, and the data ages before anyone acts on it. When the team does decide what to change, someone returns to Ads Manager to update campaigns, ad sets, budgets, and audiences by hand. As a result, teams judge campaigns on metrics alone, and the path from insight to action stays slow and manual. Today, AWS Quick added a Meta ads AI connector. The connector gives Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Meta ads customers can use natural language to create, manage, and analyze campaigns within Quick, while staying connected to the Meta ad management network. Marketers can complete tasks with support from AI, such as pulling insights to understand ads performance, creating product catalogs, and editing existing or creating new campaigns. Quick can also combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to create dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows. “Meta ads AI connector through Quick gives our marketing teams one place to go from campaign planning to execution. It lets us act on business insights directly in our ads, without the handoffs and tool switching that slow campaigns down. With fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models in the same workflow, we’ll test more creative ideas and spend more time reaching customers.” — Tina Sang, Head of Marketing at fal Demo: Meta ads in Quick The video shows how to install the Meta ads connector from Customize > Connectors in AWS Quick, sign in with Facebook, and choose which Pages, Businesses, and Instagram accounts AWS Quick can access. title: New in AWS Quick: More capable flows, an updated web experience, and agents that work together
abstract: Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done: Build, see, and improve business processes, all through conversation. Describe a process in chat and Quick builds a flow to orchestrate agents, skills, and tools with access to structured data, knowledge, and apps. New deterministic steps help make your workflows consistent and verifiable, now with longer-running workflows and support for large data volumes. Triage your day and keep agents working in the Quick web app. The updated web app puts what needs your attention and a daily briefing on your home screen, adds the agents and skills you use on desktop, and keeps your work running after you close the tab. Complete work spanning multiple agents through a single prompt. With multi-agent orchestration, several specialized agents work on your request at the same time, and Quick combines what they find into one response. Bring more of your data into Quick. Connect to Meta ads and Amplitude, then ask in natural language and combine the answers with your other sources. Skills on web, security and governance improvements, and more languages: Turn the way you do a task into a skill Quick can reuse, now in the Quick web app. Set configurable content safety and sensitive-information controls for user prompts. Support for Japanese, German, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), and Vietnamese. AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away. Turn one person’s process into your team’s process AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most important work. title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
abstract: Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache ” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks. This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro , Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer. Why a skill for KV caching and what can it do? The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simplifies this evaluation and the setup, and guides your coding agent through the following best practices before changing anything: A fit check before any spend. The agent reads your GPU fleet with a read-only describe-instances call and counts Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) interfaces. It asks only for what it can’t see: engine, model, tensor-parallel (TP) size, KV data type, server price, and how often prompts repeat. It stops and explains when something doesn’t fit. Numbers from your workload. For short prompts, loading KV state can take longer than computing it again. Above a certain prompt length (the cutover point), the read wins. That cutover and how often your prompts repeat decide whether the cache is worth its price. The agent estimates savings from your own traffic with KVTrace, at no additional charge, and stops if they don’t cover the cache’s cost. Every number says where it came from. Manage configuration across inference servers with the stack you already run. It keeps your routing and the engine’s settings and sets the servers in your inference fleet to one KV ID mechanism (hash and seed) and an explicit KV data type. Matching settings avoid key mismatches, where each server writes KV state the others can’t find. Implements best practices. title: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
abstract: Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do. We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance. In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them. A declarative foundation for Slurm cluster operations We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. The following figure shows the six layers. Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration , administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts in CreateCluster and UpdateCluster requests, and connect an external accounting database . HyperPod updates partition settings while preserving other controller-node Slurm customizations. AMI-based configuration replaces routine setup scripts with images preconfigured with Slurm, Docker, Enroot, Pyxis, and home directories. A custom AMI or OnInitComplete script handles organization-specific software. Continuous provisioning for Slurm retries capacity requests in the background; AMI-based configuration works with it , minimum capacity requirements let teams specify MinInstanceCount, and cluster operations track scaling requests. Automatic topology management maintains the network layout as nodes scale or are replaced. On Slurm 25.11 or later, partition-level topology supports tree or block topology per partition. For hardware health, on-demand deep health checks stress GPUs and test NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) connectivity, while deep health checks with continuous provisioning run as nodes are provisioned. Nodes under check stay in Slurm maintenance reservations until checks finish, keeping jobs off them. Introducing cluster extensions The five layers described so far are configurations that HyperPod can derive or apply once, when it provisions a node. The sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, behaves differently because it keeps changing for the life of the cluster. title: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters
abstract: During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it. In Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway , we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters. Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1. The challenge: Capacity spread across clusters and Regions Models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions. Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself. That choice has costs: Uneven load. During peaks, requests queue in one Region while GPUs in the other Region are idle. Manual failover. When a cluster fails, an engineer changes configuration to move traffic away from it. Custom plumbing. Spreading traffic across Regions means building and maintaining load balancers, DNS, and cross-Region networking yourself. The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own. Key benefits The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate. Put idle GPUs to work. During a peak, requests overflow to clusters with available capacity in the same Region or another one, instead of queuing on a saturated cluster. Fail over automatically. When a cluster fails, the gateway moves its traffic to the next-best cluster. Clients don’t change anything. Use one endpoint for everything. Clients call a single SageMaker-managed endpoint instead of tracking one endpoint per cluster or per model. Skip the custom networking. You don’t build or maintain load balancers, DNS, or cross-Region networking. Stay private by default. Every request is authenticated with SigV4 and IAM, and it reaches your clusters only over AWS PrivateLink. Customer feedback “At Bagelcode, we run our own LLM inference service on AWS to help teams across the company, including our game teams, use AI to improve how they work. In our beta tests, the Global Inference Gateway in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod routed requests across two AWS Regions through a single endpoint and kept serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave our small platform team cross-Region failover without having to build or maintain our own routing layer.” — Jinhyung Park, VP (AI Platform), Bagelcode How it works Setting up the gateway takes two decisions: which clusters to open up for routing, and which of them to group behind one gateway. title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
abstract: This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline. Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs. Governing AI with the framework you already have Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar. “At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.” — Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases. How the assessment works Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting. Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria. With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them. title: Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents
abstract: Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing. They turn scanned files and paper forms into structured data their systems can act on. As generative AI has matured, these organizations want more than accurate text extraction. They want to describe the information they need in their own words and get dependable, auditable answers from complex documents. Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights , a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. With Amazon Textract Insights, you describe the fields you want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. You receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training required. The challenge of extracting data from mixed packets Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files. A mortgage file, for example, typically arrives as a single scan holding a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a page of handwritten notes. Each has its own layout and appears in no fixed order. Claims files and onboarding packages can look very similar: typed forms, dense tables, scanned receipts, and free-text letters interleaved in one file. Teams usually take one of two approaches, and each has trade-offs. The first is a custom pipeline that combines optical character recognition, document splitting, classification, a foundation model prompt, and a review step. The team must integrate, scale, and operate all of it. The second is a general-purpose large language model used by default. It returns fluent answers but does not reliably cite the source page or give a confidence score. Without a traceable source and a calibrated score, it is hard to know which values to accept automatically and which to review. This uncertainty often limits how far teams can automate. Amazon Textract Insights is built for reliable document processing, bringing this entire workflow into a single asynchronous request on Amazon Textract. Rather than assembling and operating a custom pipeline, your team works through one managed API and moves directly to the data it needs. How Amazon Textract Insights works With Amazon Textract Insights, you define what to extract in a blueprint. A blueprint is a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description of what to find. Each field also has an inference type that determines whether the value is read verbatim from the page or inferred from the content of the document. You can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. You can also author your own blueprint for the documents specific to your business. For a mixed packet, you add the blueprints for each document type you expect to the same project. You then submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and enable splitting. Amazon Textract Insights splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each one to the blueprint that fits it, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value. For example, suppose you receive a mortgage application as a single 26-page PDF that contains a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer’s handwritten notes. You create an Amazon Textract Insights project with the AWS public W-2, payslip, and bank statement blueprints, add a custom blueprint for loan officer notes, and enable splitting. You then submit the file from your Amazon S3 bucket with a single StartDocumentInsights call. Amazon Textract Insights splits the file into its individual documents, matches each one to its blueprint, and writes the results to your S3 bucket. title: Introducing enhanced infrastructure observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: Large-scale model training is one of the most expensive workloads you can run on GPUs, and a single unhealthy accelerator can stall an entire distributed job. When training throughput drops, the hard part is rarely noticing that something is wrong. It is figuring out why and where. Teams often spend hours or days sifting through logs and disconnected dashboards to decide whether a slowdown came from a throttled GPU, a saturated network link, or a stalled data pipeline on the host. Today, we are announcing enhanced observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a new capability that helps you diagnose GPU training issues faster. It brings together diagnostic and profiling capabilities for training workloads that run on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Slurm orchestrators: Diagnostic summary uses Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock, and flags GPUs that deviate from their peers. Static diagnostic rules surface common failure patterns such as GPU hardware faults (XID errors, ECC memory errors), EFA throughput drops, thermal throttling, and overheating, so you catch degradation before it affects training. Why you need it Distributed training is expensive, and small inefficiencies compound into significant wasted GPU hours. Until now, getting visibility into HyperPod infrastructure meant stitching together separate tools, and even then, the metrics told you that performance had degraded without telling you why. Enhanced observability closes three gaps. It isolates a single bad accelerator across hundreds or thousands of GPUs whether through XID errors, ECC memory faults, or thermal throttling, so you spend time on the fix instead of the search. Together, these capabilities reduce troubleshooting time and help you keep expensive accelerators busy. How it works Each capability targets a different layer of a distributed training job. Default and advanced metrics Enhanced observability collects telemetry at two levels: Default metrics (enabled automatically) cover cluster health, CPU/disk/OS-level usage, GPU utilization and temperature, and per-job resource utilization. These metrics are collected every 30 seconds and sent to your chosen metric store with approximately 1–2% CPU overhead and 250–300 MB of memory. Advanced metrics (opt-in) provide deeper visibility: Full node exporter suite: comprehensive host-level metrics. All NVIDIA GPU DCGM and AWS Neuron metrics: detailed accelerator telemetry including clock speeds, power, PCIe activity, and error indicators. Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) metrics: network interface throughput, drops, retransmissions, and errors. Advanced metrics are optional because they increase the volume of telemetry sent to your metric store, which has a cost implication. Most customers running small jobs on small clusters may not need them, but they are essential for long-running training jobs on large clusters where patterns emerge over time. Metric stores You can choose between two metric stores: Amazon CloudWatch (new default) provides native monitoring through CloudWatch SageMaker Insights, so you can visualize metrics without leaving the AWS Management Console. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus for teams that standardize on Prometheus and Grafana for observability. Previously, only Prometheus was supported. CloudWatch is now the default, offering lower pricing compared to Amazon Managed Service Prometheus and tighter integration with the SageMaker console. Diagnostic summary The diagnostic summary uses two complementary approaches to surface issues across your HyperPod cluster. GPU outlier detection uses CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare GPUs within a training job across utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, and SM clock frequency. title: What Happened to Silicon Valley?
abstract: On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above. It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision. Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain. That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong? The web I thought we were building in 1993 But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill. My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN , the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way. Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind. The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. title: This Week in AI: AI’s Next Reality Check
abstract: AI’s growing role in business is exposing challenges that new models alone can’t solve. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined restrictions on autonomous agents, NVIDIA’s leadership crisis, and research into making AI systems more reliable. Agentic commerce is running into resistance Anthropic is turning Claude into a broader workplace platform. Alongside its upgraded Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 models, the company introduced Claude Meetings and Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data . Anthropic also expanded its enterprise offerings with self-hosted agent infrastructure . Companies can connect agents to internal systems while keeping credentials and session histories on their own infrastructure, even though the models still run through an external provider. OpenAI is bringing more of the shopping process into ChatGPT. Its new business profiles let companies manage how customers discover them, while business agents can answer questions and recommend products. The company also introduced ChatGPT Wallet , which allows agents to make purchases without accessing customers’ actual payment card details. Users still need to review and approve these transactions before payment. Bringing business discovery and payments into ChatGPT puts OpenAI in more direct competition with search engines and online marketplaces. Airlines, banks, and retailers, however, are already restricting outside agents. United Airlines is blocking unauthorized agents from booking flights, while financial institutions and retailers, including Amazon and eBay , have imposed their own limits. Their concerns include privacy, security, and unintended purchases. An agent may be technically capable of completing a transaction but prohibited from accessing the service. Developers will need to account for those limits, while businesses that allow such transactions must establish who bears responsibility when an agent makes an unintended purchase. NVIDIA faces a test of leadership and governance NVIDIA founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports of personal relationships that prompted an investigation into potential national security concerns. US authorities have been investigating whether a Chinese businesswoman involved in the controversy had intelligence ties to Beijing. Those allegations remain unproven. NVIDIA’s board launched its own investigation, and longtime CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. NVIDIA’s influence over the AI chip market makes its leadership transition especially consequential for customers and investors. Huang led the company for 33 years and helped establish its dominant position in AI infrastructure. Now Kress and the board must maintain customer confidence while navigating the investigation. We also discussed NVIDIA’s investments in other AI companies and the circular financing arrangements that have raised concerns about how the industry measures growth. Any changes to those investments could affect companies that depend on NVIDIA for both computing infrastructure and capital. NVIDIA’s leadership transition also raises questions about succession at founder-led technology companies. After three decades with Huang at the helm, the board must show it can provide independent oversight and maintain the company’s direction through a period of uncertainty. How NVIDIA manages that transition could offer lessons for other AI companies whose identities remain closely tied to their founders. title: Claude Watermarks Your Words, and You Can’t Check Them (Yet)
abstract: I love using AI as a writing tool. But like I wrote in “ Why Does AI Write Like Yoda? ,” it’s not because AI is a good writer. In fact, it’s pretty bad at writing, and I edit absolutely everything it generates, so the end result is basically unrecognizable compared to what it created. Unfortunately, just because AI is, on average, a pretty lousy writer, that doesn’t stop people from using AI to write all sorts of things that people end up reading, and that’s how we end up with slop. That’s where watermarking comes in. If AI-written text carries a hidden signal that a machine can pick up, someone could build slop filters with it and add a little friction to mass-producing AI text and stuffing it into every nook and cranny of the internet and, maybe, manage to keep some spaces on the internet for people. (Anthropic and OpenAI give a more official reason: the EU AI Act now requires them to mark AI-generated content in a way machines can read. I don’t know how they feel about slop.) The upshot is that almost everything Claude writes now carries a hidden watermark. A slop filter needs a way to check for the watermark. And, unfortunately, for the time being, only the big AI companies and a few organizations they’ve approved can check for it. Anthropic’s support page on marking AI-generated content now reports all of its newest models, and some older ones, watermark their text on every surface where you can use Claude, worldwide. (Bruce Hopkins covered what Anthropic announced here on Radar .) Google has used a text watermark in its Gemini app since 2024, and in October OpenAI announced it’s adding one to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU. But none of those companies lets the public check text with its detector. (Google’s synthid.com lets anyone check images, video, and audio for its watermark, including images made with ChatGPT, but it won’t let you check text from any AI lab.) I’ve read articles about watermarking, but I didn’t really know much about how it worked. So I did what any good developer would probably do: I took a shot at reasoning about it, and I came up with what I thought was a plausible way watermarking could work, based on what I know about how large language models work. And, strangely enough, it turned out I was basically right, and not because I’m some sort of amazing genius. It’s because watermarking is actually pretty straightforward, and if you know how the output part of an LLM works, you can probably design a decent watermarking system yourself. The reason I’ve got such a big interest in how models work right now is my next O’Reilly book, a deep dive into how models work called Be the Model , which we’re planning on releasing early next year. I’ve spent a lot of time over the last year thinking really hard about how to explain the internals of LLMs, and it turns out that you don’t need to understand most of the parts inside a model to see how watermarking works. All you need is the very tail end. So let’s try an experiment. I’m going to describe the relevant bits of how models work, and then, before I explain how watermarking works, I want you to take a guess and see how close you come. The only part of the model you need There’s a lot of stuff that happens inside a model. You’ve probably heard of transformer blocks, and you might know what a context window is. That’s all part of the whole machine. But at its core, a model is a next-word-predicting machine: You feed it a bunch of text as context, and it predicts the next word. The part that matters for watermarking is what goes into that machine and what comes out. What goes into the machine is tokens . We all know that when you pay an API bill, you pay some number of dollars per million tokens, but we don’t always explain what a token is. title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
abstract: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. title: The Download: inside the quest to make our minds immortal
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars. In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it. Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever. AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?” Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.” It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.” There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
abstract: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land. The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access. With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses. title: “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science
abstract: At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US). These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements. These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “ race science ” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas , recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism. Read full article Comments

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report. title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
abstract: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com . Read full article Comments

title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
abstract: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act. In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.” Shared envelopes Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges. Read full article Comments

title: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain
abstract: SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year. For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX's deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon. Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX's existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship. Read full article Comments

title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
abstract: The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons. Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing : The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts. CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications." title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
abstract: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week. The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week. "Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday . "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information." Read full article Comments

title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
abstract: When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change. "We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained." If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year. Read full article Comments

title: US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop
abstract: The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA's effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved. The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic. Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN . Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20. Read full article Comments

title: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space
abstract: Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers. The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. title: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone
abstract: Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation's most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports . Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. title: Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings
abstract: Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate . This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes , some of which are challenging prediction markets , while others are trying to get in on the action themselves. In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal" in Florida. title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
abstract: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Read full article Comments

title: 디자인 시스템 만들던 디자이너가 3D 그래픽을 그린다면
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스 Visual Designer 권윤입니다. 저는 토스에 Platform Designer로 입사해 디자인 시스템인 TDS를 만들어왔어요. 디자인 토큰 체계를 만들고 컴포넌트를 설계하는 일이 주된 업무였어요. 그러다 지난 4월, Interaction Designer, Graphic Designer 등 각자의 전문성을 가진 분들과 함께 Visual Designer라는 하나의 직무로 합쳐졌어요. 솔직히 처음에는 심란했습니다. 직무 이름이 바뀐다고 하루아침에 눈길을 사로잡는 비주얼을 만들 수 있는 건 아니니까요. 저는 디자인 시스템을 만들며 정돈되고 일관된 화면을 그려온 사람이었어요. 패턴으로 정리되는 디자인에는 익숙했지만, 처음 보는 순간 시선을 붙잡는 비주얼은 늘 다른 분들의 영역이라고 생각했어요. 이럴 때 AI의 도움을 받으면 된다고들 해요. 하지만 AI는 정해진 규칙 안에서 6~7점짜리 결과물을 빠르게 만드는 데 강합니다. 제품의 비주얼을 끌어올리는 데 필요한 두 가지는 AI가 잘하는 일이 아니라고 생각했어요. 1️⃣ 새롭게 느껴질 것 2️⃣ 시각적 완성도가 매우 높을 것 뛰어난 비주얼이 딸깍 한 번으로 나오기는 어려워요. 그렇다면 정돈된 UI만 그려온 디자이너도 AI와 함께 새롭고 완성도 높은 비주얼을 만들 수 있을까요? 이 글은 통장 개설 화면 하나에서 시작해, AI와 함께 익숙한 도구 밖으로 나가 본 기록입니다. 돌고 돌아 통장으로 저의 미션은 통장 개설을 강조하는 UI를 그리는 것이었어요. 처음 그렸던 시안을 보여드릴게요. 여러 화면을 그렸지만 모두 비슷해 보이죠. 계좌 목록 카드 아래에 '토스 통장 만들기' 한 줄을 붙이고, 붙이는 방식만 바꿔 봤을 뿐이었어요. 저는 디자인 시스템을 만들며 정돈된 UI를 그리는 일이 익숙했습니다. 익숙한 도구 안에서 그리다 보니, 상상할 수 있는 것도 딱 그만큼이었죠. 이때 여러 피드백을 받았습니다. 화면에 ‘강약’이 필요한데, ‘약’만 있는 것 같다. 더 과감한 시도가 필요하다. 유저들은 직관에 의해 행동한다. 직관적인 비주얼이 필요하다. 피드백을 받고 나니, 지금 시안을 다듬는 걸로는 부족하다는 게 분명해졌어요. 필요한 건 완전히 새로운 아이디어였어요. 토스에서는 ‘아오박’이라고 불러요. Out of the box, 틀을 벗어나는 디자인이라는 뜻이에요. 틀을 벗어날 생각만 하면 머리가 아팠습니다. Platform Designer는 사실 틀에서 벗어난 디자인보다는, 패턴화할 수 있는 디자인을 만드는 사람에 가깝거든요. 직무 통합 이후에도 저는 이 틀에서 벗어나지 못하고 있었습니다. 이때 AI와 함께 틀에서 벗어난 디자인을 찾기 위한 아이데이션을 해 봤습니다. AI는 제가 떠올리지 못한 메타포를 쏟아냈어요. 플러그를 꽂듯 새 통장을 연결하고, 고리로 계좌를 이어 붙이고, 봉투에 담거나 지갑의 빈칸에 끼워 넣는 식이었죠. 분명 제 머리로는 나오지 않았을 아이디어들이었어요. 하지만 하나도 마음에 들지 않았어요. 퀄리티도 아쉬웠지만, 더 큰 문제는 메타포였어요. '통장을 만든다'는 의미가 한눈에 들어오지 않았거든요. 틀에서 멀어질수록 직관에서도 멀어지고 있었어요. 돌고 돌아 도착한 답은 오히려 통장 그 자체였습니다. 통장은 있는 그대로 보여 주고, 그 모습에 의외성을 더하는 게 바로 이해되면서도 눈길을 끄는 비주얼이 될 것 같았어요. AI의 도움으로 빠르고 값싼 실패를 겪어 방향을 다잡을 수 있었죠. 멋진 통장을 그려보자 이제 통장을 어떻게 그릴지가 문제였어요. 처음에는 손에 익은 방법부터 시도해 봤습니다. 표현의 한계가 명확했고, 반드시 3D 그래픽이 필요하다고 느꼈습니다. 그래서 코드로 그래픽을 만들어 보기로 했어요. 코드로 3D 그래픽을 만드는 방법은 크게 두 가지예요. Three.js 같은 3D 라이브러리를 쓰거나, WebGL/Metal 같은 그래픽 API 위에서 셰이더(GPU에서 화면의 픽셀을 계산하는 작은 프로그램)를 직접 작성하는 방법이에요. 처음에는 Claude Fable 5로 WebGL 셰이더를 작성했습니다. 이후 여러 모델과 구현 방식을 병렬로 시도해 본 뒤, GPT-6 Astra가 iOS Metal 코드로 구현한 결과물을 발전시켜 보기로 했습니다. 여전히 아쉬운 퀄리티였지만, 기존에 시도했던 방법들보다 확실히 나았습니다. 또 코드는 AI가 가장 잘 다루는 언어이다 보니, 계속해서 퀄리티를 높여갈 수 있겠다는 확신이 있었습니다. 7점짜리 초안을 10점으로 만들기 1. 표지 가장 먼저, 통장 비주얼의 핵심인 표지 디자인을 디벨롭했어요. 실제 물성을 재현한 3D 통장에 디지털에서만 활용할 수 있는 애니메이션이 합쳐진다면 새로움이 느껴질 거라고 생각했어요. 이번에도 여러 AI 모델과 함께 방향성을 탐색해 봤죠. 단시간에 홀로그램 그래픽, 수채화 같은 표현, 도트 패턴, 반짝이는 표현 등 다양한 느낌을 시도해 볼 수 있었어요. 그중 셰이더를 활용한 그라디언트 애니메이션을 선택했습니다. 종이 통장의 사실적인 물성 위에, 그라디언트 애니메이션이라는 디지털 질감을 더하면 과하지 않게 의외성을 주기에 적절할 거라고 판단했습니다. 방향성을 정한 뒤에는 디테일을 다듬었어요. AI로 디자인할 때 가장 비효율적인 부분은 수정 하나하나를 말로 표현해야 한다는 점입니다. 그래서 그래픽에 있는 변수들을 슬라이더로 직접 조정할 수 있게 했어요. 작은 커스텀 에디터를 만든 셈이죠. AI가 만든 초안에서 출발해 컨트롤로 디테일을 직접 다듬으며 완성도를 높였습니다. 2. 모델링 다음으로 통장 자체의 형태와 질감을 다듬었습니다. 처음에는 AI의 결과물에서 어색한 부분을 말로 하나씩 짚어 줘도 원하는 결과가 나오지 않았습니다. 의도를 명확히 전달했다고 생각했는데도, 3D 그래픽을 프롬프트만으로 개선하기는 어려웠습니다. 더 사실적인 표현을 위해 다양하게 지시했지만 AI는 계속 부자연스러운 방향으로만 결과를 가져왔어요. 그래서 이미지 자료를 활용해 피드백해 봤습니다. 토스에 이미 있던 3D 자산의 색감, 빛과 종이 질감 표현 참고하기 Higgsfield(이미지 생성 AI)로 생성한 실물 통장의 입체감 및 빛 표현 참고하기 이미지 위에 고칠 부분을 직접 그려서 지시하기 AI가 만든 결과를 스스로 캡처하고 녹화해서 한 장면씩 확인하고, 이상한 부분을 직접 고치게 하기 참고 자료로 방향을 잡고 눈으로 확인하는 과정을 거치며 점차 의도에 가까운 모습이 나오기 시작했어요. 3. 움직임 통장의 형태를 어느 정도 잡고, 움직임을 넣으려고 했어요. 바람에 살랑이는 듯한 움직임에서 시작해, 통장을 펼치고 유저의 이름을 적어 주는 장면까지 추가했어요. 제가 기획한 움직임은 “통장이 빙글 돌며 등장하고, 이후 통장이 열리며 유저의 이름이 써진다”였어요. 처음에는 이런 모습이었습니다. 구현된 결과물은 제가 말한 조건들은 모두 담아냈지만, 눈으로 보니 아쉬운 퀄리티였죠. 이때도 통장이 얼마나 회전하는지, X, Y, Z 축마다 어떤 각도로 착지하는지를 각각 컨트롤로 만들어 조절하며 디테일을 다듬었습니다. 큼직한 움직임을 잡은 뒤에는 ‘인터랙션 스킬’로 통장뿐 아니라 화면 전체의 등장 시퀀스를 다듬었습니다. 인터랙션 스킬은 토스의 인터랙션 원칙을 AI가 읽고 따를 수 있게 정리해 둔 지침이에요. 원래는 버튼이나 화면 전환 같은 UI 모션을 위해 만들어진 스킬이었어요. 그런데 그 안에는 “이렇게 움직여라”뿐 아니라 “왜 그렇게 움직여야 자연스러운지”도 담겨 있었습니다. 예를 들어 “현실 세계의 움직임과 닮아야 자연스럽다”, “여러 요소 사이에 시간차를 두어야 리듬이 생긴다” 같은 원리요. 이 원리를 화면 전체에 적용했어요. 처음에는 모든 요소들이 일정한 속도로 한꺼번에 드러나서 움직임이 밋밋했어요. 배경, 카드, 통장, 그 아래 버튼이 차례로 자리 잡도록 시간차를 뒀습니다. 통장도 같은 원리로 다듬었어요. 딱딱하게 돌던 움직임에 스프링 모션을 입히자 훨씬 사실적으로 움직이게 됐어요. 아직 제품에 출시되지는 않았지만, 완성한 통장 그래픽을 사내 디자이너들에게 공유했을 때 반응이 좋았어요. 3D 그래픽을 전문으로 해 오신 분들에게도 좋은 반응을 얻었고, 어떻게 만들었냐는 질문도 많이 받았어요. 그래픽을 코드로 만들어 둔 덕분에
